# Heart rate recovery: 7m30 recording


## Test your predictions using the second dataset: 7m30 recording

### Explore the data

```{r explore-recording-7m}
# Read the pulse data (timestamp in Unix ms, value in bpm)
pulse_7m <- read_csv("data/pulse7m30.csv")

# Check the column names, first rows and number of measurements
names(pulse_7m)
head(pulse_7m)
nrow(pulse_7m)
```

```{r convert-time-7m}
# Sort by time, convert timestamps to minutes since the start,
# and rename the heart rate column
hr_7m <- pulse_7m |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  transmute(time_min = (timestamp - min(timestamp)) / 60000,
            hr = value)
```
# Check the converted data and the range of each variable
head(hr_7m)
summary(hr_7m)

# Check the time between two measurements (in seconds)
summary(diff(hr_7m$time_min) * 60)
```

The recording contains 91 heart rate values over 7.4 minutes, about one value every 5 seconds. Heart rate ranges from 123 to 156 bpm.

### Identify the exercise and recovery periods

As for the 3h10 recording, there are no activity labels, and the body-position signal only contains "unknown". We therefore used the acceleration signal again. Because the recording is short, we computed the motion (SD of the acceleration magnitude) over 15-second windows instead of one minute.

```{r identify-periods-7m}
# Use the first pulse timestamp as the common time origin
t0_7m <- min(pulse_7m$timestamp)

# Compute body motion per 15 s (SD of the acceleration magnitude)
motion_7m <- read_csv("data/acceleration_7m.csv") |>
  mutate(time_min = (timestamp - t0_7m) / 60000,
         magnitude = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2),
         window = floor(time_min * 4) / 4) |>
  group_by(window) |>
  summarise(motion = sd(magnitude))

# Time at which the large movements stop
t_still_7m <- 5.5

# Show this time on the motion signal
ggplot(motion_7m, aes(x = window, y = motion)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_still_7m, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time (min)", y = "Motion (SD of acceleration, g)")
```

The person moved during most of the recording (motion around 0.2–0.27 g), with only a short pause at about 1.25 minutes. The movements stopped at about 5.5 minutes, after which motion stayed below 0.1 g. Heart rate was highest at the very beginning (155–156 bpm) and decreased immediately, so the exercise itself ended before the start of the recording. We therefore considered the whole recording as post-exercise recovery, with $t = 0$ at the first measurement. However, this is not a recovery at rest: the person kept moving until about 5.5 minutes.

### Extract and visualise heart rate as a function of time

```{r plot-heart-rate-7m}
# Plot heart rate over the full recording and mark the end of the movements
ggplot(hr_7m, aes(x = time_min, y = hr)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_still_7m, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time (min)", y = "Heart rate (bpm)")
```

Heart rate decreased quickly from about 155 bpm to about 131 bpm during the first 1.5 minutes. It then stayed around 131–135 bpm while the person was still moving. After the movements stopped (dashed line), it decreased again to about 124–129 bpm.

### Identify the period corresponding to post-exercise recovery

```{r extract-recovery-7m}
# The whole recording is used as recovery, time already starts at 0
hrr_7m <- hr_7m |>
  mutate(t = time_min)

# Check the number of measurements and the time range
nrow(hrr_7m)
range(hrr_7m$t)
```

The recovery period contains the 91 measurements and lasts 7.4 minutes.

### Fit appropriate mathematical models to the recovery data

We fitted the same three models as for the 3h10 recording, with $t$ in minutes.

```{r fit-models-7m}
# Fit the linear model
m_lin_7m <- lm(hr ~ t, data = hrr_7m)

# Fit the mono-exponential model
m_mono_7m <- nls(hr ~ hr_rest + a * exp(-t / tau),
                 data = hrr_7m,
                 start = list(hr_rest = 130, a = 25, tau = 1))

# Fit the bi-exponential model
# Without limits, the slow time constant grows without end, so we limited
# the fast one to 0.05-2 min and the slow one to 2-7.5 min (recording length)
m_bi_7m <- nls(hr ~ hr_rest + a1 * exp(-t / tau1) + a2 * exp(-t / tau2),
               data = hrr_7m,
               start = list(hr_rest = 125, a1 = 20, tau1 = 0.7, a2 = 10, tau2 = 5),
               algorithm = "port",
               lower = c(hr_rest = 0, a1 = 0, tau1 = 0.05, a2 = 0, tau2 = 2),
               upper = c(hr_rest = 200, a1 = 100, tau1 = 2, a2 = 100, tau2 = 7.5))

# Display the fitted parameters
summary(m_lin_7m)
summary(m_mono_7m)
summary(m_bi_7m)
```

The linear model gave $HR(t) = 143.7 - 2.54\,t$. The mono-exponential model gave $HR_0$ = 130.2 bpm, $A$ = 27.2 bpm and $\tau$ = 1.08 min (about 65 s). These values are physiologically plausible: heart rate starts at about 157 bpm and approaches 130 bpm.

Without limits, the bi-exponential fit did not give usable values: the slow time constant increased to extremely large values (and its amplitude too), so that the slow component simply behaved like a straight line. With the limits, the slow time constant stopped exactly at the upper limit (7.5 min), and the fast component (A₁ = 22.1 bpm, τ₁ = 0.75 min) was close to the mono-exponential one. This means that the 7.4-minute recording does not contain enough information to estimate a second, slower time constant, and the values of the slow component depend on the limit we chose.
